main_risk: Off-manifold worlds might actually help as hard exploration (the DR philosophy), reversing the prediction.

territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
one_line: DR's gains are largely predictable from gradient variance across randomized copies of the same scene, revealing it as a variance-reduction technique measurable before full training
problem: There is no cheap predictor of how much a given randomization configuration will help transfer; every configuration change requires full training runs to evaluate.
core_hypothesis: DR works by exposing the model to nuisance-varied copies of identical content, and its benefit is governed by how much the induced gradient variance across copies covers the sim-to-real perturbation directions; a pre-training statistic (gradient dispersion across randomized copies, projected against sim-real feature differences) predicts final transfer gains across DR configurations.
why_important: Reduces DR configuration search from many full trainings to cheap probe measurements, and provides mechanistic clarity on what DR actually optimizes.
why_possibly_novel: DR theory exists in expectation-over-domains formulations; an operational pre-training predictor based on copy-wise gradient geometry appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Transfer may hinge on rare randomization events (tail draws) invisible to variance statistics computed over typical copies.
default_community_belief: DR configurations must be evaluated by end-to-end training; no intermediate statistic is trusted as a surrogate.
falsifiable_prediction: Across 8+ DR configurations, the copy-gradient-dispersion statistic computed on a probe network will rank final transfer performance with high correlation, and configurations matched on the statistic but differing in nominal axis count will transfer equivalently.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate randomized copy-sets under 8 configurations; compute the statistic on a small probe; train full models; test rank correlation and the matched-statistic equivalence.
fastest_falsification: Compute the statistic for 3 configurations with known transfer results from prior sweeps; rank agreement in this retrospective check gates further investment.
main_risk: Probe-scale gradient geometry may diverge from full-model geometry, degrading the prediction exactly for the expensive configurations of interest.

territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
one_line: Randomizing nuisances the target domain holds fixed (e.g., viewpoint for a mounted camera) actively costs accuracy: fixed-nuisance identification should precede any DR design
problem: DR pipelines randomize every available axis, including ones that are constant in the deployment (camera height for a fixed installation, lighting for an indoor line), a systematic mismatch nobody prices.
core_hypothesis: Invariance to a deployment-constant nuisance strictly discards usable information (the model could have exploited the constancy as context); for fixed-camera deployments, viewpoint-randomized training will measurably underperform viewpoint-fixed training with matched data volume, with the deficit concentrated in classes that benefit from the stable geometry prior.
why_important: Establishes deployment-variance profiling as a mandatory first step of DR design, replacing the randomize-everything default with a matched-invariance principle.
why_possibly_novel: DR papers report what randomization helps; the deliberate demonstration of randomization harm on deployment-constant axes with the class-level mechanism appears missing.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Position priors may contribute negligibly once appearance features are strong, making the insurance genuinely free.
default_community_belief: Extra invariance is harmless insurance; randomizing an axis the target holds fixed costs nothing.
falsifiable_prediction: On fixed-camera evaluation, viewpoint-fixed synthetic training will beat viewpoint-randomized training at matched budgets, and the gap will grow for classes whose recognition depends on position-in-frame priors, while on multi-camera evaluation the ordering reverses.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One procedural scene set rendered {fixed viewpoint, randomized viewpoint}; evaluate on fixed-camera real data and on multi-view real data; compare orderings and class-level deltas.
fastest_falsification: The two-arm viewpoint experiment on one fixed-camera dataset; a null gap refutes the harm claim for the most intuitive axis.
main_risk: Fixed-camera real evaluation sets with sufficient class diversity may need to be assembled from surveillance-style datasets with licensing constraints.

territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
one_line: The correct unit of randomization is the scene, not the image: within-scene appearance randomization (same layout, many appearances) teaches layout-invariant features faster than across-scene randomization
problem: DR pipelines randomize parameters per rendered image, conflating two different training signals: appearance variation of identical content versus content variation, whose distinct effects are never separated.
core_hypothesis: Presenting the same scene under many appearances provides aligned contrastive structure (identical labels, varied nuisances) that teaches nuisance invariance more sample-efficiently than the same appearance diversity spread across different scenes, where nuisance and content variation are confounded; matched-budget comparisons will show within-scene randomization reaching target invariance and transfer levels with fewer total images.
why_important: Gives DR a two-knob design theory (scene coverage vs variant depth) with an optimum, directly actionable in every rendering pipeline's sampling loop.
why_possibly_novel: The scenes-vs-variants trade appears in passing in dataset papers; its framing as implicit contrastive alignment with an invariance-acquisition-rate mechanism appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: SGD may not exploit within-scene alignment without an explicit contrastive objective, making grouping genuinely immaterial.
default_community_belief: Total image count and randomization width determine DR value; how variation is grouped across scenes is immaterial.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched render budgets, corpora organized as (fewer scenes x more appearance variants) will yield higher measured nuisance invariance and better sim-to-real transfer than (more scenes x fewer variants) up to a scene-diversity floor, below which layout coverage collapses and the ordering reverses, yielding a predictable interior optimum.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fixed budget corpora at 5 scene/variant splits; train identical models; measure invariance probes and real-domain transfer; locate the optimum and test its stability across two targets.
fastest_falsification: Two extreme splits at small scale with invariance probes; no invariance-rate difference means the alignment mechanism is inert.
main_risk: The optimum's location likely depends on layout complexity of the target, complicating a clean general statement.

territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
one_line: Curriculum DR (narrow-to-wide randomization ranges) avoids the early-training underfitting that wide-from-start DR causes, reaching better transfer at equal budget
problem: DR applies full-width randomization from step zero, though early training may be unable to extract signal from maximally varied data, wasting the early budget.
core_hypothesis: Wide randomization at initialization slows the formation of basic task features (the model sees mostly nuisance variance before it can represent content), so widening ranges progressively as competence grows preserves early learning speed while reaching the same final invariance, dominating fixed-width DR at matched total steps.
why_important: A schedule-only DR improvement with a clean mechanistic signature, plus the pretrained-backbone prediction gives a practical rule for when curricula matter at all.
why_possibly_novel: Curricula over difficulty exist broadly; range-scheduling for randomization width with the pretrained-backbone dissociation test appears specific and untested for segmentation DR.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern optimizers with warm-up may already absorb the early difficulty, leaving no deficit for the curriculum to fix.
default_community_belief: Randomization width is a static dataset property; scheduling it is an unnecessary complication.
falsifiable_prediction: Progressive-widening schedules will reach higher real-domain transfer than fixed-wide schedules at matched budgets, with learning-curve analysis showing the fixed-wide arm's deficit accumulating specifically in the early phase, and no deficit when starting from a pretrained backbone (competence already present).
minimal_falsification_experiment: From-scratch and pretrained backbones x {fixed-wide, progressive} schedules at matched budgets on one sim-to-real pair; compare final transfer and early learning curves.
fastest_falsification: The pretrained-backbone cell alone: if fixed-wide matches progressive there but loses from scratch, the mechanism is confirmed cheaply; if fixed-wide never loses, the idea dies.
main_risk: Schedule hyperparameters (widening rate) add a tuning dimension that could unfairly favor either arm if not searched symmetrically.

judge_flags.note: Keep-with-note: kept because the pretrained-backbone dissociation (no deficit when competence is already present) directly tests the early-underfitting mechanism; without that arm this is a curriculum-schedule permutation and should be treated as mutate.

territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
one_line: A large share of DR's transfer benefit is reproducible by test-time augmentation ensembling on a non-randomized model, identifying which randomization axes truly need training-time exposure
problem: DR requires expensive re-rendering and retraining per configuration, but for some nuisance axes its effect may be equivalent to simply averaging predictions over input perturbations at inference.
core_hypothesis: For photometric axes, DR's benefit approximates marginalization over nuisances, achievable post hoc by test-time augmentation (TTA-ensembling) with matched perturbation families; for geometric/structural axes, training-time exposure changes representations in ways inference-time averaging cannot mimic, so an axis-by-axis equivalence audit will split axes into 'deferable to test time' and 'training-essential'.
why_important: Axes deferable to test time need no rendering or retraining, collapsing DR's cost for a known subset of nuisances and clarifying what training-time DR uniquely contributes.
why_possibly_novel: TTA and DR are separately mature; the systematic equivalence audit framing (which randomization can be moved to inference) appears unexamined.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Training-time randomization may improve features even for photometric axes (better minima), leaving TTA structurally short everywhere.
default_community_belief: DR's benefits require training-time exposure by definition; inference-time tricks are a separate, weaker category.
falsifiable_prediction: TTA-ensembling over photometric perturbations on a non-DR model will recover a large fraction of photometric DR's transfer gain, while TTA over geometric perturbations will recover little of geometric DR's gain, producing a stable axis classification across two dataset pairs.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train {no-DR, photometric-DR, geometric-DR} models; evaluate no-DR under matched photometric/geometric TTA-ensembling; compute recovered fractions per axis type.
fastest_falsification: Photometric recovered-fraction measurement on one pair (one no-DR model, one DR model, one TTA evaluation); low recovery ends the deferability claim.
main_risk: TTA inference cost scales with ensemble size, so 'equivalence' must be qualified by compute budget to be fair.

territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
one_line: Adversarially chosen randomization parameters (worst-case rendering per scene, selected by current-model failure) matches uniform DR's transfer with an order of magnitude fewer rendered images
problem: Uniform randomization spends most of its render budget on parameter draws the model already handles, and active-selection alternatives are untested at the rendering-pipeline level for segmentation.
core_hypothesis: Model failures concentrate in small regions of randomization-parameter space; a closed-loop pipeline that searches, per scene, for parameter draws maximizing current-model loss and renders only those, will match uniform DR's final transfer using a small fraction of the renders, with the efficiency ratio growing as training progresses and failure regions shrink.
why_important: Rendering is the cost center of synthetic pipelines; a validated active-rendering loop changes the economics of DR for every simulation-based team.
why_possibly_novel: Active DR exists conceptually in RL and robotics control; a rendering-in-the-loop implementation for dense-prediction transfer with quantified render savings appears untested.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Loss-guided selection may repeatedly mine the same failure family, collapsing diversity and underperforming uniform sampling at scale.
default_community_belief: Uniform coverage of randomization space is the safe and standard sampling policy; per-sample selection is not worth the loop complexity.
falsifiable_prediction: Matched-transfer comparisons will show the active pipeline requiring several-fold fewer rendered images than uniform sampling, and ablations replacing loss-guided search with random search under the same loop will lose most of the efficiency, confirming the selection mechanism.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement the loop on a procedural pipeline with cheap re-rendering; compare renders-to-target-transfer curves of active vs uniform vs random-search arms on one sim-to-real pair.
fastest_falsification: Small-scale loop with an early stopping comparison: if active does not beat uniform in renders-to-fixed-transfer by at least 2x at small scale, the order-of-magnitude claim is implausible.
main_risk: Worst-case draws may be adversarial artifacts (renderer edge cases) that teach nothing about reality, poisoning the loop.

judge_flags.reason: Active/adversarial domain randomization exists in RL and robotics; as framed the contribution is the ported rendering-in-the-loop pipeline plus an efficiency headline (10x fewer renders), a mechanical transfer to dense prediction.
judge_flags.mutation: Make the failure-geography claim primary: measure whether and how model failures concentrate in small, stable regions of randomization-parameter space (loss landscapes over the parameter space, region shrinkage over training, renderer-artifact contamination per the stated risk); the active pipeline is the exploit of that measured structure.

territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
one_line: Segmentation domain shift factorizes into sensor, appearance, geometry, and layout tiers with a strict transfer-difficulty ordering, testable by constructing single-tier shifts
problem: Domain shift for segmentation lacks an agreed decomposition, so methods, benchmarks, and claims are incomparable: each paper's 'domain gap' mixes different shift kinds in unknown proportions.
core_hypothesis: Shifts can be organized into four tiers (sensor/ISP, surface appearance, object geometry, scene layout); holding all else fixed and shifting one tier at a time in a controlled synthetic environment will reveal a strict difficulty ordering (sensor easiest to adapt, layout hardest), stable across architectures, because each tier requires changes at increasing network depth.
why_important: A validated shift taxonomy with difficulty ordering would give the field a coordinate system: benchmarks could report tier composition, methods could declare tier scope, and results would finally compose.
why_possibly_novel: Informal tier language is everywhere; a controlled single-tier construction with calibrated magnitudes and the depth-correspondence test appears never executed.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The tiers may not be separable even in simulation (layout changes alter shading and occlusion), undermining single-tier construction.
default_community_belief: Domain gap is a scalar; decompositions are narrative devices rather than measurable structure with stable orderings.
falsifiable_prediction: Single-tier constructed shifts of calibrated magnitude will produce transfer drops with the predicted ordering across architectures, and each tier's drop will correlate with adaptation-required depth (measured by which layers must be fine-tuned to recover performance).
minimal_falsification_experiment: In a procedural world, construct four single-tier shift pairs matched by a common magnitude scale (feature-space distance); train, transfer, and measure recovery-depth profiles per tier.
fastest_falsification: Build just the sensor-tier and layout-tier pairs and check the predicted extreme ordering; a reversal ends the taxonomy's core claim.
main_risk: Calibrating 'equal magnitude' across qualitatively different tiers is the crux and could be contested whichever scale is chosen.

territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
one_line: Dense prediction breaks classification-derived domain-generalization theory because errors propagate spatially: one shifted region corrupts its neighborhood through receptive fields, violating i.i.d.-example bounds
problem: Theoretical guarantees and intuitions for learning under shift assume independent examples; segmentation's unit of failure is a spatially extended region whose influence spreads, and no empirical characterization of this propagation exists.
core_hypothesis: Under partial-image shift (a shifted patch or region within an otherwise in-domain image), errors extend beyond the shifted region by a distance governed by effective receptive field size, so total error grows super-linearly with shifted-region area, and architectures with larger context aggregation show more propagation despite better in-domain accuracy, a measurable robustness-accuracy structure classification theory does not predict.
why_important: Establishes the empirical law connecting spatial context use to shift fragility, informing both architecture selection for deployment under shift and the correct statistical unit for dense-prediction shift theory.
why_possibly_novel: Effective receptive fields and shift robustness are separately studied; the error-propagation law with halo measurement as a shift-robustness predictor appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Context aggregation may help reject shifted regions (using surrounding evidence) rather than spread their corruption, inverting the halo prediction.
default_community_belief: More context is better: global context aggregation is treated as uniformly beneficial, including under shift.
falsifiable_prediction: Splicing controlled shifted regions into test images will show error halos around shifted regions with radius scaling with architecture receptive field, and per-architecture halo size will predict full-image shift degradation better than in-domain accuracy does.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct spliced-shift test sets; measure error-halo radii across 4 architectures (CNN small/large context, transformer variants); correlate halo size with full-shift degradation.
fastest_falsification: Single-architecture spliced-region test with halo measurement; presence or absence of halos beyond the region boundary is immediately visible.
main_risk: Splicing borders introduce artifacts that create their own halos, requiring careful blending controls.

territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
one_line: Part of the sim-to-real gap is a label-convention artifact: relabeling real evaluation data under the synthetic geometric convention shrinks the measured gap without changing any model
problem: Synthetic labels are geometric truth (exact projections), real labels are annotator conventions (simplified polygons, class-boundary customs); measured 'gaps' conflate model failure with convention mismatch, and the conflation has never been sized.
core_hypothesis: A quantifiable fraction of reported sim-to-real gaps comes from convention mismatch rather than model error; this fraction varies by class (large for amorphous boundaries like vegetation, small for rigid objects) and can be measured by dual-convention relabeling of a modest evaluation subset.
why_important: Every sim-to-real paper's headline number contains this artifact in unknown proportion; sizing it would recalibrate progress claims and motivate convention-explicit benchmarks.
why_possibly_novel: Label-convention issues are acknowledged qualitatively; the dual-convention interaction design that isolates and sizes the artifact appears unexecuted.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The convention component may be a few tenths of a point, real but negligible against multi-point domain gaps.
default_community_belief: Ground-truth labels are convention-free; measured gaps reflect model and domain properties only.
falsifiable_prediction: On a dual-labeled evaluation subset (annotator convention vs geometric convention), synthetic-trained models will score systematically higher under the geometric convention while real-trained models score higher under the annotator convention, with the interaction effect sizing the convention component of the gap per class.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Dual-label 200 real images under both conventions with written protocols; evaluate matched synthetic-trained and real-trained models under both; estimate the interaction per class.
fastest_falsification: Evaluate both model types with boundary-tolerance bands of increasing width as a convention-insensitivity proxy; convergence of gaps at small tolerances would suggest a small convention component without any relabeling.
main_risk: Producing a faithful 'geometric convention' for real images is expensive and partially ill-defined for fuzzy materials.

judge_flags.note: absence-of-prior-work stated without literature search; treat why_possibly_novel as HYPOTHESIS, not fact (judge_C JC2-QA-02)

territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
one_line: Shift effects compose predictably: performance under combined shifts is a simple function (approximately multiplicative in survival terms) of single-shift performances, enabling a 'shift algebra' for deployment forecasting
problem: Deployments face combined shifts (night + rain + new city), but evaluation only ever covers single shifts; without a composition rule, coverage of the combinatorial shift space is impossible.
core_hypothesis: For shifts acting through different mechanisms (photometric, weather, geographic), degradation composes approximately multiplicatively in retained-performance terms (retained(A+B) = retained(A) x retained(B)), with systematic deviations only for same-mechanism pairs (interference) and information-destroying pairs (floor effects), so a small set of single-shift measurements forecasts most combined conditions.
why_important: Would collapse the combinatorial evaluation burden of deployment certification into linear cost (measure singles, compute combinations), a practical foundation for safety cases under compound shift.
why_possibly_novel: Corruption benchmarks report singles; composition laws for shift effects on dense prediction with a mechanism-based deviation taxonomy appear unproposed.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Nonlinear failure thresholds (mode collapse of predictions under compound stress) may make any smooth composition rule useless precisely in the dangerous regimes.
default_community_belief: Combined shifts are unpredictable emergent conditions requiring direct evaluation; no composition law is expected to hold.
falsifiable_prediction: Across a grid of shift pairs and triples on segmentation benchmarks, the multiplicative rule will predict combined retained-mIoU within a small tolerance for cross-mechanism combinations and fail in the predicted directions (over/under-prediction) for same-mechanism and floor cases.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct 6 single shifts spanning 3 mechanisms; evaluate a fixed model zoo on all singles, 15 pairs, and selected triples; fit and test the multiplicative rule with deviation analysis.
fastest_falsification: One model, two cross-mechanism shifts, three evaluations (A, B, A+B); a large multiplicative-rule violation in the benign case ends the strong version immediately.
main_risk: Composition may be model-dependent (robust models compose differently), fragmenting the law into families.

judge_flags.title: Shift algebra: combined-shift performance composes multiplicatively from single shifts

territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
one_line: Class-agnostic boundary representations transfer across domains far better than class representations: boundary-first pretraining is a domain-generalization strategy, not just an architectural choice
problem: Under strong shift, everything degrades together in standard evaluations, hiding whether some representational components are intrinsically more domain-stable and could anchor transfer.
core_hypothesis: Boundary-ownership structure (where region transitions are) is governed by domain-stable image physics (occlusion, contrast, continuity), while class identity depends on domain-specific appearance statistics; therefore boundary-detection components of segmenters will retain far more cross-domain performance than classification components, and pretraining boundary structure first (then attaching classification) will yield better shifted-domain performance than joint training at matched compute.
why_important: Identifies which part of segmentation knowledge is portable across domains, informing pretraining design, adaptation targets (adapt the classifier, trust the boundaries), and modular architecture choices for deployment.
why_possibly_novel: Edge-based pretraining exists historically; the domain-stability asymmetry claim with decomposed shift evaluation and its curriculum consequence appears untested in the modern context.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Boundary detection may rely on the same texture statistics as classification in learned models, making its apparent stability illusory outside hand-crafted-feature intuitions.
default_community_belief: Representation components degrade together under shift; there is no separable 'portable core' worth designing around.
falsifiable_prediction: Decomposed evaluation (boundary quality vs region-classification quality) across shifts will show systematically smaller boundary degradation; boundary-first curricula will beat joint training on shifted targets while matching it in-domain, across two shift families.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate boundary-vs-classification degradation for existing models across 3 shift types; then run boundary-first vs joint training at matched compute on one sim-to-real pair.
fastest_falsification: Decomposed degradation measurement on existing checkpoints across one strong shift; the asymmetry either appears or the premise dies without new training.
main_risk: Boundary quality metrics depend on class-agnostic boundary ground truth, which must be derived carefully from semantic labels to avoid circularity.

territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
one_line: Domain gap grows superlinearly with label-space granularity: fine-grained taxonomies amplify shift damage, making coarse-to-fine adaptation a principled (not just convenient) strategy
problem: Datasets differ in label granularity (road vs road/lane/shoulder), and shift studies never control for it, though granularity plausibly interacts with how much domain-specific appearance detail the task requires.
core_hypothesis: Coarse classes are separable by domain-stable cues while fine distinctions depend on domain-fragile appearance details, so the same physical shift produces disproportionately larger relative degradation at finer granularities; the degradation-vs-granularity curve is superlinear, and adapting coarse levels first then refining (hierarchical adaptation) beats flat adaptation at matched budget.
why_important: Explains benchmark incomparability (gaps measured at different granularities are not commensurable), and yields a practical adaptation schedule grounded in the granularity-fragility law.
why_possibly_novel: Granularity effects on accuracy are known in-domain; the interaction of granularity with domain shift as a lawful superlinear amplification appears unmeasured.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Fine distinctions might rely on geometry (lane markings are shapes) that is domain-stable, flattening or inverting the curve for some hierarchies.
default_community_belief: Domain gap is a property of the image domains; the label space is an orthogonal design choice that scales difficulty uniformly.
falsifiable_prediction: Evaluating fixed shifts across nested label hierarchies (2, 8, 20, 60 classes derived from one dataset) will show relative mIoU degradation increasing superlinearly with class count, and hierarchical adaptation will beat flat adaptation on the finest level across two shift types.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One dataset with a label hierarchy; construct nested tasks; evaluate transfer under 2 shifts at each granularity; fit the degradation-vs-classes curve; run hierarchical-vs-flat adaptation on the finest task.
fastest_falsification: Two-granularity comparison (coarse vs fine) under one shift with frequency-matched classes; the relative-degradation ratio either exceeds unity clearly or the amplification claim fails.
main_risk: Class count confounds class rarity (finer classes are rarer); needs frequency-controlled analysis to isolate granularity itself.

territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
one_line: The domain-pair abstraction is wrong for deployment: shift arrives as ordered trajectories, and method rankings from pairwise benchmarks invert under trajectory evaluation
problem: All standard shift benchmarks evaluate source-to-target pairs, while real deployments experience continuous ordered drift (seasons, sensor aging, gradual geographic rollout); whether pairwise rankings predict trajectory performance is unknown.
core_hypothesis: Methods differ in trajectory-relevant properties invisible to pairwise evaluation (error accumulation under sequential adaptation, recovery after transient shifts, hysteresis); constructing ordered-shift evaluations from existing data (temporal orderings, severity ramps) will show method rankings substantially different from pairwise rankings, with self-training-based methods specifically vulnerable to error accumulation on trajectories.
why_important: If pairwise benchmarks mispredict deployment behavior, the field's evaluation standard needs a trajectory tier; the result would define it and expose which method families are deployment-safe.
why_possibly_novel: Continual test-time adaptation exists as a subfield; the explicit rank-instability claim against pairwise benchmarks with directional predictions for method families appears untested.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Trajectory performance may be dominated by average pairwise difficulty along the path, keeping rankings stable and the pairwise abstraction adequate.
default_community_belief: Pairwise source-target evaluation is an adequate proxy for deployment shift; trajectory effects are second-order.
falsifiable_prediction: Rank correlation between pairwise and trajectory evaluations of the same method suite will be low, with predicted directional flips (accumulating methods fall, stateless methods rise), reproducible across two trajectory constructions.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build 2 trajectory benchmarks (severity ramp on corruptions; temporal ordering of a multi-season dataset); evaluate 6 methods pairwise and on trajectories; compare rankings.
fastest_falsification: Evaluate 3 methods on one severity-ramp trajectory vs endpoints-only; a strong ranking agreement in this minimal case deflates the instability claim.
main_risk: Trajectory construction choices (speed of drift, transients) may themselves determine rankings, requiring sensitivity analysis for credibility.

territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
one_line: Per-class texture-vs-shape cue reliance measured on the source domain predicts per-class sim-to-real transfer without any target labels: a cue-reliance audit as a transfer forecast
problem: Per-class transfer outcomes are unpredictable before target data exists, so synthetic-data teams cannot prioritize which classes need more assets, randomization, or real anchors.
core_hypothesis: Texture cues are domain-fragile and shape cues domain-stable; a per-class cue-reliance score (measured on source data via cue-conflict stimuli or texture-scrambling sensitivity) will predict per-class sim-to-real IoU drops with useful accuracy, because transfer failure is concentrated where reliance on fragile cues is highest.
why_important: Provides a pre-deployment, target-free forecasting tool at class granularity, directly actionable in synthetic-data budgeting, and links the shape/texture-bias literature to transfer prediction quantitatively.
why_possibly_novel: Shape/texture bias is studied at whole-model level; per-class reliance measurement used as a class-granular transfer predictor with intervention validation appears new.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Per-class drops may be driven by target-side factors (class frequency, context change) that no source-side measurement can see.
default_community_belief: Per-class transfer is empirically idiosyncratic; class-level forecasts without target data are not considered feasible.
falsifiable_prediction: Across two synthetic-to-real pairs, per-class cue-reliance scores will rank per-class transfer drops with strong correlation, and interventions that shift specific classes toward shape reliance (targeted texture randomization) will improve exactly those classes' transfer, confirming the causal direction.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute per-class cue-reliance on source-trained models via texture-scrambled and style-swapped source images; measure per-class transfer drops on real targets; test rank correlation; run targeted-randomization intervention for the 3 most texture-reliant classes.
fastest_falsification: Reliance-vs-drop scatter for one dataset pair using existing checkpoints; a flat scatter ends the forecasting claim.
main_risk: Cue-conflict construction for dense prediction (per-region style swaps) is technically finicky and may inject artifacts that distort reliance scores.

territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
one_line: ImageNet-style pretraining helps domain adaptation mostly through texture-statistics coverage, not semantics: label-free texture-corpus pretraining matches it for segmentation transfer
problem: Supervised classification pretraining is the default initialization for segmentation transfer pipelines, and its benefit is attributed to semantic knowledge, steering pretraining investment toward more labels.
core_hypothesis: For transfer under domain shift, the operative contribution of large-scale pretraining is exposure to broad natural-image texture and color statistics (which stabilizes early-layer features across domains); pretraining on label-free corpora engineered for texture-statistics coverage (no object semantics, e.g., texture crops and natural patches) will match classification pretraining for downstream shifted segmentation, while both beat from-scratch, isolating statistics coverage as the mechanism.
why_important: If statistics coverage is the active ingredient, cheap unlabeled texture corpora replace expensive labeled pretraining for shift-robust segmentation, and pretraining design should optimize coverage metrics rather than label count.
why_possibly_novel: Ablations of pretraining exist (SSL vs supervised); a deliberately semantics-free, coverage-engineered pretraining arm designed to isolate the statistics mechanism for shift robustness appears untested.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Semantic pretraining may specifically help under shift by providing category priors robust to appearance change, exactly what texture corpora cannot supply.
default_community_belief: Pretraining transfers semantic knowledge; its benefit under shift reflects generalizable object understanding.
falsifiable_prediction: Texture-coverage pretraining will land within a small margin of classification pretraining on shifted-target segmentation across two pairs, and the residual advantage of classification pretraining will concentrate in classes requiring semantic disambiguation (visually similar classes), quantifying the semantic component.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Pretrain matched backbones on {classification corpus, semantics-free texture corpus, nothing}; fine-tune identically for segmentation; evaluate on shifted targets with class-stratified analysis.
fastest_falsification: Small-scale pretraining comparison (texture-corpus vs classification at reduced scale) on one shifted pair; near-parity or a large gap appears at small scale already.
main_risk: Constructing a genuinely semantics-free corpus with matched scale and diversity is difficult; residual object content would contaminate the isolation.

territory: Synthetic data + domain shift (generation-for-segmentation, sim-to-real, distribution shift science)
one_line: Sim-to-real transfer is bottlenecked by the decoder, not the encoder: frozen synthetic-trained encoders with real-data-tuned decoders recover most of the gap, localizing where domain knowledge lives
problem: Adaptation methods treat the whole network as domain-contaminated, but the actual locus of sim-to-real failure within the encoder-decoder division has never been established, leaving intervention design unguided.
core_hypothesis: Synthetic-trained encoders learn largely domain-transferable features (geometry, contours, coarse texture classes), while decoders overfit domain-specific decision rules (exact boundary placement conventions, class-appearance thresholds); therefore swapping or lightly tuning only the decoder on limited real data will recover a disproportionate share of the sim-to-real gap, while the reverse (tuning only the encoder) recovers little at matched parameter budget.
why_important: Localizing the gap turns adaptation from whole-network retraining into a small-decoder problem, cutting real-data needs and compute, and gives theory a concrete structural claim about where domain specificity resides in dense-prediction networks.
why_possibly_novel: Partial fine-tuning is common practice, but a systematic locus-of-gap study with matched parameter budgets and the pretraining-scale interaction prediction appears missing for sim-to-real segmentation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Early-layer texture statistics are exactly where synthetic and real images differ most, which argues the encoder is the true bottleneck, reversing the prediction.
default_community_belief: Domain shift contaminates features throughout the network; encoders trained on synthetic data are considered the primary carriers of domain bias.
falsifiable_prediction: In matched-budget partial-tuning experiments, decoder-only tuning will recover most of the achievable gap closure while encoder-only tuning recovers a small fraction, and the asymmetry will persist across architectures and grow with the amount of synthetic pretraining data (better encoders, equally biased decoders).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Synthetic-pretrained models at 2 pretraining scales; real-data budgets {1%, 10%}; arms {decoder-only, encoder-only, full tuning} at matched trainable parameters; compare recovered fractions.
fastest_falsification: Decoder-only vs encoder-only tuning at 1% real data on one pair; the asymmetry direction is visible in two runs.
main_risk: The encoder-decoder division is architecture-dependent; results may not translate across families (CNN vs transformer decoders).

judge_flags.title: Sim-to-real gap is decoder-localized, not encoder-localized

judge_flags.note: absence-of-prior-work stated without literature search; treat why_possibly_novel as HYPOTHESIS, not fact (judge_C JC2-QA-02)

one_line: Super-resolving images before segmentation improves mask plausibility while decreasing fidelity to the true scene, because predicted boundaries snap to hallucinated edges.
problem: SR preprocessing is routinely added ahead of segmentation for low-resolution inputs and evaluated by aggregate mIoU, without testing whether the gains reflect recovery of the true scene or agreement with generator-invented structure.
core_hypothesis: SR output pulls segmentation boundaries toward edges the generator invented; agreement with the ground truth of the true high-resolution scene degrades in locally ambiguous regions even as boundary smoothness and plausibility improve.
why_important: SR preprocessing is being adopted operationally in satellite, surveillance, and medical pipelines; if boundaries are systematically displaced toward fabricated evidence, downstream area and length measurements are biased rather than merely noisy, and more data will not fix it.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: SR utility is usually reported as aggregate metric change; conditioning boundary displacement on local SR residual magnitude as an explicit mechanism test appears less explored, pending literature search.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern segmenters may rely mostly on mid-frequency shape cues and ignore the high-frequency detail SR fabricates, making the displacement effect negligible in practice.
default_community_belief: SR preprocessing is a safe, generally beneficial enhancement step for low-resolution segmentation inputs.
falsifiable_prediction: On paired LR/HR datasets, boundary F-score of SR-then-segment will be lower than segment-LR-then-upsample-mask specifically in regions of high SR residual (where SR output diverges most from true HR), with error magnitude increasing monotonically with local residual.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take one paired LR/HR segmentation dataset, run one pretrained SR model and one frozen segmenter both ways, stratify boundary displacement by local SR residual, and test for the predicted monotonic relation.
fastest_falsification: Half-day analysis with off-the-shelf SR and segmenter on one paired dataset; no training required.
main_risk: SR residual correlates with intrinsic scene difficulty, confounding the stratification; matched-difficulty controls or residual manipulation at fixed content are needed.

one_line: MMSE-optimal denoising selectively erases low-contrast thin structures, so denoising can raise PSNR while lowering thin-class segmentation recall.
problem: Denoisers are trained to minimize mean squared error, which drives ambiguous low-SNR content toward the local mean; whether this systematically deletes the faint thin structures (wires, vessels, cracks) that segmentation needs is rarely quantified.
core_hypothesis: For structures whose contrast is near or below the noise floor, MMSE denoising is equivalent to structure deletion; segmentation recall on thin classes therefore drops after denoising even when full-image PSNR and SSIM improve.
why_important: Denoising is treated as a monotone quality improvement; a contrast-dependent deletion regime would mean preprocessing choices silently trade thin-class recall for cosmetic quality in safety-relevant pipelines like vessel and crack inspection.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: the MMSE-attenuation argument is classical signal processing, but a quantitative deletion threshold expressed in units of structure contrast over noise sigma, validated against segmentation recall, appears not to be standard practice.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Segmenters trained with heavy augmentation may already fail on sub-noise-floor structures, so denoising would remove nothing the model could use anyway.
default_community_belief: Denoising strictly helps downstream analysis whenever the input is visibly noisy.
falsifiable_prediction: Across noise levels, thin-structure recall of a frozen segmenter will be higher on noisy inputs than on denoised inputs once structure contrast falls below a measurable multiple of the noise sigma, while large-object IoU shows the opposite ordering.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Synthesize thin structures at controlled contrast into real noisy backgrounds, denoise with two standard models, and plot segmenter recall versus contrast-to-noise ratio for noisy versus denoised inputs.
fastest_falsification: One-day synthetic contrast-sweep experiment with pretrained denoisers and a pretrained segmenter.
main_risk: Synthetic insertions may not capture real thin-structure statistics; a follow-up on a real vessel or crack dataset with noise added is needed for external validity.

one_line: Restoration models pretrained on natural images impose natural-scene priors that misinterpret domain-specific structures as artifacts and remove them.
problem: Off-the-shelf restoration models are increasingly applied to scientific and industrial imagery whose statistics differ from natural photographs, but the direction of the induced bias is not characterized.
core_hypothesis: Structures that are rare in natural-image statistics (isolated bright puncta, periodic grids, hairline defects) are treated by natural-image-trained restorers as noise or artifact and are attenuated or regularized away, with the attenuation predictable from the structure's likelihood under a natural-image prior.
why_important: It converts anecdotes about restoration harming scientific images into a predictive law: which structures are at risk can be computed before deployment, enabling principled go/no-go decisions for restoration preprocessing.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: linking per-structure restoration attenuation to an explicit likelihood score under a generative natural-image model, rather than reporting domain-level degradation, appears less explored.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Attenuation may be driven by local frequency content alone rather than semantic likelihood, in which case a simple spectral account beats the prior-likelihood account.
default_community_belief: Restoration failures on out-of-domain imagery are unpredictable domain-gap effects to be fixed by fine-tuning.
falsifiable_prediction: Attenuation of inserted structures after restoration will correlate with their improbability under a natural-image density model, and segmentation recall for those structure classes will drop more than for natural-looking classes at matched size and contrast.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Insert structure families of varying natural-image likelihood into photographs at matched contrast, restore with pretrained models, and regress attenuation against likelihood scores from an independent density model.
fastest_falsification: Compare attenuation predictions of a spectral baseline versus a likelihood model on one structure-insertion benchmark; if spectral wins, the hypothesis dies.
main_risk: Density estimates from available generative models may be too unreliable at patch level to give a usable likelihood axis.

one_line: Jointly trained restoration-plus-segmentation systems pass segmentation hints through the restored image as imperceptible signals rather than genuinely improving image quality.
problem: End-to-end pipelines that train a restoration front-end with a downstream segmentation loss report gains, but the mechanism is assumed to be better image quality rather than covert channel coding between the two networks.
core_hypothesis: The restoration module learns to embed segmentation-relevant side information as low-amplitude patterns tuned to its paired segmenter, analogous to reported steganographic behavior in image-to-image translation; the restored images are not better inputs for independent segmenters.
why_important: If gains come from a cheating channel, joint restoration modules will fail silently whenever the downstream model is swapped or retrained, which is exactly how such pipelines are deployed in practice.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: steganographic collusion is discussed for cycle-consistent translation; a targeted test in restoration-for-segmentation pipelines with transfer and perturbation controls appears less explored.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The observed gains may survive perturbation and transfer, indicating genuine task-relevant enhancement rather than collusion.
default_community_belief: Task-driven restoration gains reflect improved effective image quality for the task.
falsifiable_prediction: Restored images from a jointly trained front-end will improve the paired segmenter substantially but transfer little or no gain to an independent frozen segmenter, and adding low-pass filtering or mild noise to the restored image will destroy the paired gain disproportionately.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train a small restoration front-end jointly with segmenter A, then evaluate its outputs with frozen segmenters B and C and under mild perturbations; compare gain retention across the three conditions.
fastest_falsification: Perturbation-sensitivity test on any published joint pipeline's outputs takes hours if checkpoints are available.
main_risk: Genuine task-tuned enhancement can also transfer poorly if segmenters differ in input statistics; the perturbation-sensitivity control is essential to separate the two explanations.

judge_flags.title: Steganographic collusion in joint restoration+segmentation pipelines

one_line: The restoration that maximizes downstream segmentation accuracy is measurably different from, and looks worse than, the restoration humans prefer.
problem: Restoration is tuned to human preference (perceptual losses, user studies) under the assumption that human-pleasing outputs are also good machine inputs.
core_hypothesis: Optimizing a restoration front-end directly for a frozen segmenter's accuracy converges to outputs with characteristic non-photorealistic signatures (exaggerated boundary contrast, suppressed texture) that humans rate as worse, revealing a systematic divergence between perceptual and task-utility optima.
why_important: It quantifies how much accuracy pipelines sacrifice by insisting on human-pleasing intermediates and motivates storing machine-facing and human-facing restorations separately.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: task-driven restoration exists, but a controlled quantification of the perceptual-cost-versus-utility-gain frontier with human raters appears less common; needs literature check.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern segmenters trained on diverse data may be near-invariant to the stylistic differences between the two optima, making the utility gap negligible.
default_community_belief: Perceptually better restorations are assumed to be better inputs for downstream vision models.
falsifiable_prediction: A restoration model fine-tuned only with downstream segmentation loss will beat a perceptually tuned model on mIoU by a clear margin while losing a two-alternative human preference test on the same images.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fine-tune one restorer with segmentation loss and one with perceptual loss from the same initialization, evaluate both on mIoU and on a small human preference study.
fastest_falsification: Skip training: compare frozen-segmenter accuracy on outputs of existing distortion-oriented versus perception-oriented SR checkpoints; if no gap exists, the strong version is falsified.
main_risk: The divergence may be small on mildly degraded natural images and only large under severe degradation, limiting generality of the headline claim.

one_line: Restoration-induced boundary shifts are directional (systematic erosion or dilation per structure type), not zero-mean noise, so they bias measurements rather than adding variance.
problem: When restoration changes segmentation output, the change is implicitly modeled as symmetric jitter; whether it has a consistent sign per structure polarity is untested.
core_hypothesis: Restoration priors favor smooth extended regions, so dark thin structures on bright backgrounds are systematically eroded and bright regions dilated; the induced boundary shift has a nonzero mean whose sign is predictable from local polarity and curvature.
why_important: Zero-mean errors average out across measurements; directional bias corrupts every area, width, and count statistic in the same direction, which matters for longitudinal and quantitative studies that assume preprocessing is neutral.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: decomposing restoration-induced segmentation change into bias and variance components conditioned on polarity appears less explored than reporting aggregate IoU deltas.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Segmenter decision thresholds may already absorb small intensity shifts, leaving no measurable directional displacement at mask level.
default_community_belief: Preprocessing-induced segmentation changes are treated as symmetric noise that ensembling or averaging can remove.
falsifiable_prediction: Signed boundary displacement between masks computed on original versus restored images will show a nonzero mean conditioned on structure polarity, consistent in sign across restoration models sharing training distributions.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On any dataset, compute signed distance between boundary points of masks from original and restored images, stratify by local polarity and curvature, and test the mean against zero with sign consistency across two restorers.
fastest_falsification: A few hours of signed-distance analysis with existing checkpoints on one dataset.
main_risk: Polarity-conditioned bias may vary strongly across restoration architectures, weakening the claim to a per-model property rather than a general law.

one_line: Segmentation networks are far more robust to texture-destroying degradations than to contour-degrading ones, inverting the texture-bias narrative imported from classification.
problem: Robustness intuitions for dense prediction are borrowed from classification studies showing CNN texture bias, but segmentation supervision explicitly rewards boundary accuracy, which may reverse the dependence.
core_hypothesis: At matched information removal, degradations that scramble texture but preserve contours (texture randomization, moderate noise) cost segmentation little, while degradations that blur or displace contours at equal perceptual severity cost disproportionately, because dense training installs shape-dominant features.
why_important: Robustness engineering (augmentation menus, restoration priorities) currently inherits classification-derived rankings; if segmentation robustness is contour-dominated, restoration effort should be reallocated toward deblurring and edge preservation rather than denoising.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: task-conditional reversal of the texture-shape robustness ordering, tested with matched backbones across tasks, appears not to be an established result; needs literature search.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Transformer-based segmenters may be texture-hungry in ways that restore the classification ordering, making the effect architecture-specific.
default_community_belief: Texture bias findings from classification transfer to dense prediction, so texture-corrupting degradations are treated as the primary robustness threat.
falsifiable_prediction: On a degradation battery equalized by human-rated severity or mutual-information proxies, contour-corrupting transforms will produce at least twice the mIoU drop of texture-corrupting transforms for segmentation models, a ratio that will not hold for classification models on the same backbone.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Apply matched-severity texture-only and contour-only corruptions to one benchmark, evaluate a segmentation model and a classification model sharing a backbone, and compare degradation ratios.
fastest_falsification: One-day corruption battery on published checkpoints for both tasks.
main_risk: Equalizing severity across corruption families is the crux; a bad severity axis makes the ratio arbitrary.

one_line: Restoration and segmentation models share the same learned natural-image prior, so their errors are correlated and cascade ensembling yields far less than independence predicts.
problem: Pipelines assume restoration errors and segmentation errors are roughly independent, so combining restored-input and raw-input predictions should average errors away; the shared-prior structure of both model families is ignored.
core_hypothesis: Because restorers and segmenters are trained on overlapping natural-image distributions, both fail on the same improbable-under-the-prior content; error overlap between segment(restore(x)) and segment(x) is therefore much higher than chance, and ensembling the two gives only marginal gains precisely on the hardest content.
why_important: Redundancy planning in deployed systems (run it raw and restored, then vote) is built on the independence assumption; demonstrating prior-induced correlation changes how safety margins for degraded-input vision should be computed.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: error-correlation analysis between restoration-preprocessed and raw pipelines, tied explicitly to shared prior probability, appears less explored than model ensembling literature.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If segmentation errors are dominated by annotation noise or class confusion rather than prior-improbable content, overlap would be high for reasons unrelated to shared priors.
default_community_belief: Running segmentation on both raw and restored inputs provides substantially independent looks at the scene.
falsifiable_prediction: Pixelwise error overlap between the two pipeline variants will substantially exceed the product of their marginal error rates, and oracle-ensemble upper bounds will show the smallest headroom in regions scored as improbable by an independent density model.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On one degraded benchmark, compute per-pixel error sets for both pipeline variants, measure overlap against the independence baseline, and stratify headroom by density-model likelihood.
fastest_falsification: Overlap-versus-independence computation on existing predictions takes hours.
main_risk: Error overlap can also arise from shared degradation severity rather than shared priors; severity must be controlled as a covariate.

one_line: The residual uncertainty of a restoration model predicts where a downstream segmenter will fail better than the segmenter's own confidence does.
problem: Failure prediction for segmentation under degraded inputs relies on the segmenter's confidence, which is known to be unreliable; the restoration stage possesses complementary information about what was unrecoverable but it is discarded.
core_hypothesis: Regions where a restoration model's output is unstable (across seeds, timesteps, or checkpoints) mark evidence-poor image areas; these instability maps localize downstream segmentation errors better than segmenter confidence because they measure input evidence rather than decision confidence.
why_important: It reframes failure prediction as an input-evidence problem solvable by the preprocessing stage, giving deployed pipelines an error-locator that does not require touching the segmenter.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: using restoration-stage instability as a segmentation error localizer, rather than as an image-quality diagnostic, appears less explored; not primarily a calibration contribution but an information-routing one.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Segmenter confidence, for all its flaws, sees task-relevant features that restoration variance cannot, and may dominate once boundary proximity is controlled.
default_community_belief: The segmentation model itself is the natural and best source of information about where it will fail.
falsifiable_prediction: Ranking pixels by restoration instability will retrieve segmentation errors with higher area under the sparsification curve than ranking by segmenter softmax confidence, on degraded inputs across at least two datasets.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate multi-seed diffusion restorations for one degraded dataset, compute per-pixel output variance, and compare error-retrieval curves against segmenter confidence baselines.
fastest_falsification: Sparsification-curve comparison with an off-the-shelf diffusion restorer, one day including sampling.
main_risk: Restoration instability and segmenter confidence may both track trivial boundary proximity, requiring distance-to-boundary matching to show any nontrivial advantage.

one_line: Downstream segmentation accuracy versus SR upscaling factor is non-monotonic, peaking below the native resolution at the onset of hallucination.
problem: Practitioners assume that super-resolving closer to native resolution is monotonically better for downstream tasks, so pipelines default to the largest available SR factor.
core_hypothesis: As SR factor increases, genuine detail recovery saturates while hallucination grows, so task utility follows an inverted-U; the peak location is predictable from the SR model's per-factor residual statistics on held-out paired data.
why_important: A predictable utility peak turns SR-factor selection from folklore into measurement, and directly contradicts the more-resolution-is-better default baked into pipeline design.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: per-factor utility curves exist in scattered ablations, but a systematic non-monotonicity claim with a predictive rule for peak location appears untested; literature check required.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Segmenters may downweight fabricated high-frequency content enough that utility simply saturates rather than declines.
default_community_belief: Super-resolving to the highest available factor before analysis is the safe default.
falsifiable_prediction: Sweeping SR factors (2x, 4x, 8x) on the same LR inputs will show segmentation accuracy peaking at an intermediate factor for high-degradation inputs, with the peak shifting toward higher factors as input quality improves.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One paired dataset, one SR family with multiple factors, one frozen segmenter; plot utility versus factor at three input degradation levels.
fastest_falsification: Factor-sweep evaluation with existing checkpoints, roughly one day.
main_risk: The non-monotonicity may only appear with generative SR models and vanish for regression-based SR, restricting the claim's scope.

one_line: When annotations are drawn on enhanced or restored views, models trained on raw images inherit the enhancement model's hallucinations through the labels.
problem: Annotation tooling commonly shows enhanced, denoised, or contrast-adjusted views to annotators, but the trained model consumes raw images; the label-side contamination path from restoration hallucination into ground truth is unexamined.
core_hypothesis: Labels created on restored views encode boundary placements and structure completions that exist only in the restored image; models trained raw-image-to-such-labels learn to predict the restoration model's biases, effectively distilling the restorer through the annotation channel.
why_important: It identifies a contamination pathway that survives even perfectly raw training pipelines, implying dataset documentation must record the annotation viewing transform as a first-class provenance field.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: annotation-view provenance as a vector for restoration-bias inheritance appears undocumented in dataset audit literature; needs search.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Annotators may rely on shape priors robust to the viewing transform, so the labels would differ mainly in noise, not in systematic restoration bias.
default_community_belief: Ground-truth quality depends on annotator skill and protocol; the image rendering shown during annotation is treated as irrelevant.
falsifiable_prediction: For a dataset annotated twice (on raw views and on restored views), a model trained on restored-view labels will reproduce restoration-specific structures on test images where the restorer hallucinates, at a rate significantly above a raw-label-trained model.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Re-annotate a small subset of one dataset on raw and enhanced views, train small models on each label set, and test for restoration-signature structures in predictions on held-out hallucination-prone images.
fastest_falsification: Compare existing labels against raw versus enhanced image evidence on a dataset whose annotation protocol is documented; measurable in days without new annotation if protocol metadata exists.
main_risk: Dual annotation is costly and inter-annotator variance may swamp the view effect at small scale.

one_line: Low-light enhancement style acts as a semantic class prior: the same pixels receive different class labels depending on which enhancement network prepared the image.
problem: Low-light segmentation pipelines treat enhancement as visibility correction, assuming class decisions depend on scene content rather than on the enhancement network's stylistic choices.
core_hypothesis: Enhancement networks impose learned illumination and color statistics that shift ambiguous regions across class decision boundaries; class flips between enhancement styles are systematic per class pair (e.g., road versus sidewalk) rather than random.
why_important: If preprocessing style shifts semantics, benchmark comparisons of night segmentation methods that use different enhancers conflate segmentation ability with enhancement style, and deployment behavior changes when an enhancer is updated.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: enhancement is usually evaluated by downstream accuracy; characterizing the class-flip structure it induces as a systematic prior appears less explored.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern segmenters heavily augmented with color jitter may be invariant to enhancement style, leaving flip rates near noise level.
default_community_belief: Enhancement improves visibility uniformly and does not change what things are, only how visible they are.
falsifiable_prediction: Running one frozen segmenter on outputs of three different enhancement models over the same night scenes will produce class-flip matrices that are significantly structured (repeatable class pairs) rather than uniform, and the flip structure will be predictable from each enhancer's color transfer statistics.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Three pretrained enhancers, one segmenter, one night-driving dataset; compute cross-enhancer class-flip matrices and test for structure against a permutation baseline.
fastest_falsification: One-day inference-only study with existing checkpoints.
main_risk: Flips may concentrate on a few genuinely ambiguous classes, making the finding real but of limited scope.

one_line: Segmentation models trained on JPEG-compressed data learn the 8x8 block grid as a boundary prior, measurably snapping mask edges to block boundaries.
problem: Most large segmentation datasets are stored as JPEG, embedding a fixed periodic artifact structure into training images; whether models internalize the block grid as a spatial prior is untested.
core_hypothesis: Block-boundary gradients act as weak but persistent edge evidence during training; trained models therefore place mask boundaries on the 8-pixel grid at above-chance rates, especially in low-contrast regions, and this bias transfers to uncompressed test images.
why_important: A grid-locked boundary prior is a dataset-format artifact contaminating every boundary-precision claim at the 1-3 pixel scale, exactly the scale where modern methods now compete.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: JPEG effects on classification are studied; a positional mod-8 analysis of segmentation boundary placement appears not to exist; literature check needed.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Random crops during training decouple image coordinates from block phase, which may fully randomize the prior the model could learn.
default_community_belief: Storage compression of training data is a negligible detail below the level of augmentation noise.
falsifiable_prediction: The histogram of predicted boundary positions modulo 8 will deviate from uniform for JPEG-trained models on PNG test images, with the deviation growing as local image contrast decreases, and shrinking for models trained on losslessly stored data.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate two public segmenters on lossless imagery, compute boundary-position histograms modulo 8 stratified by local contrast, and compare against a model trained on lossless data if available.
fastest_falsification: Boundary phase histogram on existing predictions takes hours.
main_risk: Resizing and augmentation during training may destroy grid alignment, diluting the effect below detectability.

judge_flags.note: member of convergent family 'JPEG/codec grid artifacts become learned boundary/detection priors'; deeper merge deferred to Stage 2 dedup

one_line: Motion deblurring collapses the exposure interval to an arbitrary instant, so segmenting deblurred frames localizes moving objects at a biased time point.
problem: Deblurring before segmentation is standard for motion-blurred footage, but a blurred object is a time integral; which instant the deblurred image represents, and hence where the object boundary is placed in time, is undefined and unexamined.
core_hypothesis: Deblurring networks systematically reconstruct an instant biased toward one end of the exposure (set by training data conventions), so segmented positions of moving objects carry a consistent temporal offset convertible into a spatial bias proportional to velocity.
why_important: Downstream velocity estimation, collision prediction, and tracking assume deblurred frames represent exposure midpoints; a consistent temporal bias corrupts these geometrically, and it is invisible in image-quality metrics.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: temporal semantics of deblurred outputs are discussed for extreme cases (blur-to-video), but the induced segmentation position bias as a measurable law appears unexplored.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Averaging over training data may make networks reconstruct the exposure midpoint after all, in which case the bias is zero and only variance remains.
default_community_belief: A deblurred frame is treated as the sharp image of the scene at that frame's timestamp.
falsifiable_prediction: On synthetic blur generated from high-fps video with known ground truth per instant, the deblurred-then-segmented object position will align with a consistent quantile of the exposure interval across scenes and speeds, not with the interval midpoint, and the spatial bias will grow linearly with object speed.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Synthesize blur from high-fps clips, deblur with two pretrained models, segment, and regress recovered object position against per-instant ground truth to estimate the represented time quantile.
fastest_falsification: One-day synthetic study with existing deblurring checkpoints and high-fps public video.
main_risk: Deblurring networks may be inconsistent across scenes, yielding a distribution over instants rather than a clean bias, which weakens but does not kill the claim.

one_line: Hallucinated structures in generative restoration are unstable across sampler seeds while genuinely recovered structures are stable, enabling a training-free hallucination detector.
problem: There is no accepted way to flag which parts of a diffusion-restored image are evidence-supported versus invented, blocking safe use of generative restoration in analysis pipelines.
core_hypothesis: Evidence-constrained pixels are pinned by the likelihood term and reproduce across seeds, whereas prior-driven fabrications sit in flat regions of the posterior and vary across seeds; cross-seed structural disagreement therefore localizes hallucination.
why_important: A reliable evidence map would let downstream segmentation consume generative restorations selectively, unlocking their quality benefits without inheriting fabrications in measurement-critical regions.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: seed-ensemble variance is used for uncertainty in generation broadly; validating it specifically as a hallucination localizer against paired ground truth in restoration appears less established.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Strong classifier-free guidance and low-temperature sampling can collapse seed diversity, making fabrications reproducible and the variance signal blind.
default_community_belief: Hallucination in restoration is treated as an unavoidable qualitative risk to be managed by choosing conservative models rather than something measurable per pixel.
falsifiable_prediction: On paired degraded/clean data, per-pixel cross-seed variance of diffusion restorations will rank hallucinated pixels (defined by disagreement with the clean reference) with high retrieval performance, and will beat single-output image-space heuristics like local sharpness.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Sample 8 seeds from one diffusion restorer on a paired benchmark, compute cross-seed variance maps, and measure retrieval of reference-disagreement pixels against sharpness and confidence baselines.
fastest_falsification: One-day multi-seed sampling and retrieval analysis on an existing paired benchmark.
main_risk: Consistent hallucinations (the model inventing the same structure every seed) would evade the detector precisely in the most dangerous cases; the false-negative structure must be characterized.

judge_flags.title: Seed-instability as training-free restoration-hallucination detector

one_line: Generative restoration fabricates objects preferentially at contextually plausible locations, so hallucination-induced false positives evade anomaly-based quality control.
problem: Quality control for restored imagery assumes fabrications look anomalous or out of place; the conditional structure of generative priors suggests the opposite.
core_hypothesis: Because diffusion priors model context-object co-occurrence, fabrications appear exactly where such objects are likely (a car on a road, a nucleus in tissue), so downstream segmentation false positives on restored images cluster in high-plausibility locations and pass contextual anomaly filters.
why_important: It shows that the standard safety net for restoration pipelines is structurally mismatched to the threat: the failure mode is plausible insertion, not implausible artifact, demanding evidence-based rather than plausibility-based auditing.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: hallucination studies focus on frequency and fidelity; the claim that fabrications are contextually camouflaged against QC appears untested.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Restoration conditioned on strong evidence may fabricate mostly texture rather than objects, so object-level plausible insertions could be too rare to matter.
default_community_belief: Fabricated content can be caught by human review or anomaly detection because it will look subtly wrong or out of place.
falsifiable_prediction: False-positive segments on restored images will score higher on context-plausibility models than false positives on raw degraded images, and anomaly detectors will catch a significantly smaller fraction of restoration-induced false positives than of noise-induced ones.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Restore degraded scenes with a generative model, collect downstream false-positive segments, score them with a context-plausibility model, and compare with false positives from matched non-generative pipelines.
fastest_falsification: Count object-level insertions in an afternoon by differencing restored and reference images on a paired benchmark.
main_risk: Defining and scoring context plausibility independently of the generative prior under test is delicate; a shared prior would make the result circular.

one_line: Generative restoration replaces rare structures with frequent lookalikes (mode substitution), silently collapsing rare-class recall in downstream segmentation.
problem: Restoration quality is averaged over pixels dominated by common content; what happens to rare structure categories under strong generative priors is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: When evidence is weak, diffusion restorers resolve ambiguity toward high-density modes of the training distribution, so rare classes are reconstructed as visually similar common classes; the substitution rate scales inversely with the class's prior frequency.
why_important: Rare classes are often the point of the analysis (defects, lesions, endangered species); a frequency-directed substitution bias means generative preprocessing selectively destroys the signal of interest while improving average quality metrics.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: mode-seeking behavior is known in generative modeling; its quantification as a directional class-substitution matrix affecting downstream segmentation appears less explored.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The likelihood term may dominate at realistic degradation levels, keeping substitutions too rare to measure outside extreme degradation.
default_community_belief: Restoration errors are class-agnostic image-quality issues distributed roughly evenly over content.
falsifiable_prediction: On degraded images containing rare classes, class-flip rates from rare to visually similar common classes after restoration will exceed the reverse direction by a large factor, and the asymmetry will grow with degradation severity and with guidance strength.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Degrade images of rare-class instances and matched common-class instances equally, restore, run a frozen segmenter, and compare directional flip rates.
fastest_falsification: Directional flip-rate measurement on one rare-class dataset with an off-the-shelf diffusion restorer, about a day.
main_risk: Visual similarity between class pairs must be controlled, otherwise the asymmetry could reflect classifier confusion rather than restoration substitution.

judge_flags.note: member of convergent family 'Regression-to-the-frequent: rare inputs replaced by frequent lookalikes'; deeper merge deferred to Stage 2 dedup
